[BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690) trains bidirectional attention by reconstructing masked items; next-item inference appends a reserved mask and reads its representation. Interior masks can exploit right context unavailable at the terminal mask. The original method includes last-item-only masking to reduce this mismatch. [Recency-sampling research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) also identifies weak alignment between random masking and next-item prediction. These findings motivate testing terminal-mask supervision separately from architectural locality; they do not establish that insufficient locality caused the observed behavior.

Controlled diagnostic proposal: independently vary terminal-mask training frequency and a soft relative-distance attention bias, retaining global attention within one jointly trained BERT4Rec per category. Compare interior versus terminal masked-target loss, and measure validation sensitivity to removing older versus recent history and shuffling order within those segments. Report results by history length and category. Attention mass by distance is descriptive; perturbation effects provide stronger evidence of reliance on recent or older context. A locality benefit concentrated in recent-history-sensitive cases would support the hypothesis; degradation on long histories would suggest lost longer-term information. Keep seed, training budget, candidate sets and masking settings fixed except for each ablated factor.

[Sampled-metric analysis](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) shows that sampled rankings can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation. Preserve the pinned 99-negative, seed-42 evaluator and macro validation HR@10 for selection; interpret gains as specific to that protocol. Full-catalog simulator recommendations should not be treated as equivalent evidence, and no test labels are needed for these diagnostics.
